expectedText:
PENSION APPORTIONMENT AND THE GILLMORE ELECTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Pension Apportionment and Gillmore Election Information Sheet concerns Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, whose proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties is pending, has concluded by judgment, or may be filed, in the California superior court for Sacramento County. It describes what California law says about two related questions that arise when one spouse has earned retirement benefits under a defined benefit pension plan: first, how a court decides what portion of those benefits the community owns, including the apportionment method commonly called the "time rule"; and second, what happens when the employee spouse becomes eligible to retire but keeps working — the situation addressed in In re Marriage of Gillmore (1981) 29 Cal.3d 418, from which the phrase "Gillmore election" takes its name. It states, in general terms, the rule of In re Marriage of Brown (1976) 15 Cal.3d 838 that pension rights earned during marriage are community property whether or not they are vested, the division methods Brown describes and the continuing jurisdiction they require, the apportionment discussion in In re Marriage of Lehman (1998) 18 Cal.4th 169, the choices Gillmore gives each spouse once the employee spouse is eligible to retire, the statutory limit in Family Code section 2610 on ordering a plan to pay before the member retires, the consequences Gillmore attaches to an election of immediate payment, and the rule of In re Marriage of Cornejo (1996) 13 Cal.4th 381 fixing the date from which such payments run. This information sheet does not calculate any community or separate percentage, value any pension, state whether Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee is eligible to retire, or state whether any election has been made or any motion has been filed; those are matters for the court to decide on the specific evidence before it, or for Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee to address by their own written agreement.

PENSION RIGHTS EARNED DURING MARRIAGE ARE COMMUNITY PROPERTY, VESTED OR NOT
California treats a pension right earned through employment during marriage as a property interest of the community rather than as a mere expectancy. In In re Marriage of Brown (1976) 15 Cal.3d 838, the California Supreme Court overruled French v. French (1941) 17 Cal.2d 775 and held that pension rights, whether or not vested, represent a property interest, and that to the extent those rights derive from employment during marriage they are a community asset subject to division in a dissolution proceeding. Brown also explains the specialized meaning the word "vested" carries in marital-property cases: it refers to a pension right that is not subject to forfeiture if the employment relationship ends before retirement. Under that usage a pension right may be vested — safe from forfeiture — and still not yet "matured," because the employee has not reached the point at which benefits are payable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Pension rights, whether or not vested, represent a property interest; to the extent that such rights derive from employment during coverture, they comprise a community asset subject to division in a dissolution proceeding."
  — In re Marriage of Brown, 15 Cal.3d 838, 842 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1367330/in-re-marriage-of-brown/)
  "it refers to a pension right which is not subject to a condition of forfeiture if the employment relationship terminates before retirement."
  — In re Marriage of Brown, 15 Cal.3d 838, 842 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1367330/in-re-marriage-of-brown/)
  "Throughout our decisions we have always recognized that the community owns all pension rights attributable to employment during the marriage."
  — In re Marriage of Brown, 15 Cal.3d 838, 844 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1367330/in-re-marriage-of-brown/)
  Known gap: This clause states the holding and terminology of a 1976 California Supreme Court decision; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension, and pension characterization rules differ among community property and equitable distribution states. The Brown opinion was decided under former Civil Code section 4800, the predecessor of the Family Code provisions cited elsewhere in this document, so its statutory references do not match current section numbers. All three quotations were verified against two independent fetches of the CourtListener opinion page made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets, and the first quotation was additionally confirmed by an exact-phrase search restricted to that opinion's cluster in CourtListener's public search API; no non-CourtListener copy of this 1976 opinion was obtained, because the California courts' own website does not publish slip opinions from that era. Federal law separately governs whether and how a private-sector plan may pay a former spouse, and nothing in Brown displaces those federal requirements. This clause does not state what portion of any particular pension the community owns; that is the separate question of apportionment addressed in the clause that follows on the time rule.

TWO WAYS TO DIVIDE A PENSION, AND THE JURISDICTION A DEFERRED DIVISION REQUIRES
Brown describes two general approaches a court may take to a community interest in a pension. One is to determine the present value of the pension rights and divide that value now, often by awarding the pension to the employee spouse and offsetting other community assets to the other spouse. The other is used when uncertainties affecting vesting or maturation make present valuation unsatisfactory: the court awards each spouse an appropriate portion of each pension payment as it is paid, which avoids computing present value and divides equally the risk that the pension will never vest. Brown acknowledges that an award of future pension payments as they fall due requires the court to continue jurisdiction to supervise those payments. Brown's treatment of retroactivity also turns on reserved jurisdiction: the decision states that it does not apply retroactively to permit a nonemployee spouse to assert an interest in nonvested pension rights where the marriage's property rights were already adjudicated by a decree that became final, unless the decree expressly reserved jurisdiction to divide those pension rights later.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "But if the court concludes that because of uncertainties affecting the vesting or maturation of the pension that it should not attempt to divide the present value of pension rights, it can instead award each spouse an appropriate portion of each pension payment as it is paid. This method of dividing the community interest in the pension renders it unnecessary for the court to compute the present value of the pension rights, and divides equally the risk that the pension will fail to vest."
  — In re Marriage of Brown, 15 Cal.3d 838, 848 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1367330/in-re-marriage-of-brown/)
  "As respondent points out, an award of future pension payments as they fall due will require the court to continue jurisdiction to supervise the payments of pension benefits."
  — In re Marriage of Brown, 15 Cal.3d 838, 849 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1367330/in-re-marriage-of-brown/)
  "We conclude that our decision today should not apply retroactively to permit a nonemployee spouse to assert an interest in nonvested pension rights when the property rights of the marriage have already been adjudicated by a decree of dissolution or separation which has become final as to such adjudication, unless the decree expressly reserved jurisdiction to divide such pension rights at a later date"
  — In re Marriage of Brown, 15 Cal.3d 838, 851 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1367330/in-re-marriage-of-brown/)
  Known gap: This clause states what one 1976 California Supreme Court opinion says about division methods and continuing jurisdiction; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension, and it does not state which method a court would choose in any given case — Brown leaves that choice to the trial court. The retroactivity passage quoted here concerns the retroactive reach of the Brown decision itself to dissolution decrees that were final in 1976, not a general rule about reopening judgments today; relief from a final family law judgment is governed by separate provisions addressed elsewhere in this corpus. Brown predates the Retirement Equity Act of 1984 and the qualified domestic relations order mechanism, so its description of how payments reach a nonemployee spouse does not account for the federal requirements that now apply to private-sector plans. All three quotations were verified against two independent fetches of the CourtListener opinion page made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets; no non-CourtListener copy of the opinion was obtained. Part of the first quotation also appears, as a quotation of Brown, in In re Marriage of Gillmore, and a portion of it is quoted in this corpus's separate information sheet on the division of retirement benefits and QDROs, so it is not an independent source from that document's treatment of the same point.

APPORTIONING A PENSION BETWEEN COMMUNITY AND SEPARATE ESTATES — THE TIME RULE
When a pension was earned partly during marriage and partly outside it, the benefit must be apportioned between the community estate and the employee spouse's separate estate. In In re Marriage of Lehman (1998) 18 Cal.4th 169, the California Supreme Court stated that the superior court must apportion an employee spouse's retirement benefits between the community property interest of the two spouses and any separate property interest of the employee spouse alone, that the court has discretion in the choice of methods, and that whatever method it uses the result must be reasonable and fairly representative of the relative contributions of the community and separate estates. The method Lehman describes as the one apparently employed most frequently is the time rule: the community property interest is expressed as a fraction whose numerator is the employee spouse's length of service during marriage before separation and whose denominator is the employee spouse's length of service in total, with the separate property interest being the remainder of 100 percent. Under a division of the community interest in halves, each spouse's share is one-half of the resulting community percentage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "The superior court must apportion an employee spouse’s retirement benefits between the community property interest of the employee spouse and the nonemployee spouse and any separate property interest of the employee spouse alone."
  — In re Marriage of Lehman, 18 Cal.4th 169, 187 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1242627/in-re-marriage-of-lehman/)
  "the community property interest in retirement benefits is the percentage representing the fraction whose numerator is the employee spouse’s length of service during marriage before separation, here 17.39 years, and whose denominator is the employee spouse’s length of service in total, here 32.67 years; the separate property interest is the percentage representing the remainder of 100 percent minus the community property interest percentage."
  — In re Marriage of Lehman, 18 Cal.4th 169, 176 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1242627/in-re-marriage-of-lehman/)
  "When, in a case such as this, the superior court uses the time rule, with the employee spouse’s length of service during marriage before separation in the numerator, and with the employee spouse’s length of service in total in the denominator, it arrives at a result that is “reasonable and fairly representative of the relative contributions of the community and separate estates.”"
  — In re Marriage of Lehman, 18 Cal.4th 169, 188 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1242627/in-re-marriage-of-lehman/)
  Known gap: This clause states what one California Supreme Court opinion says about apportionment method; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension, and it does not compute or assert any percentage for any person. Lehman itself notes that the choice of apportionment method rests in the trial court's discretion, so the time rule is not the only permissible approach, and Lehman states that the time rule's use is not unreasonable where the amount of the retirement benefits is substantially related to the number of years of service — a condition that is a question of fact about the particular plan. This clause also fills a gap that this corpus's existing information sheet on the division of retirement benefits and QDROs expressly disclosed: that document states it does not describe the time-rule apportionment formula. Source-quality caution: the CourtListener text of this 1998 opinion contains visible optical-character-recognition defects, rendering the words "time rule" as "time rale" in several places and "born" as "bom"; the sentences quoted here were selected from passages free of such defects and were compared character for character across two independent fetches made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets, and one quoted phrase was additionally confirmed by an exact-phrase search restricted to that opinion's cluster in CourtListener's public search API. No non-CourtListener copy of the opinion was obtained. The percentages and year figures appearing in the quoted passage are the facts of the Lehman parties' own case and say nothing about any other marriage.

A POST-SEPARATION ENHANCEMENT OF THE SAME PENSION — CHARACTERIZATION VERSUS APPORTIONMENT
Lehman also addressed what happens when an employer improves a defined benefit pension after the marriage has ended — in that case a voluntary early-retirement incentive that added putative years of service and waived an actuarial reduction. The court framed the question as whether a nonemployee spouse who owns a community property interest in an employee spouse's retirement benefits under such a plan owns a community property interest in the retirement benefits as enhanced, and answered yes. Lehman distinguishes two distinct questions: characterization, meaning whether the enhancement is a community asset at all, and apportionment, meaning to what extent it belongs to the community and separate estates. The court held that owning a community interest in the benefits carries with it a community interest in the benefits as enhanced, while cautioning that this does not mean the enhancement is a community asset in its entirety, because the extent of the community and separate shares remains a question of apportionment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Does a nonemployee spouse who owns a community property interest in an employee spouse’s retirement benefits under such a plan own a community property interest in the retirement benefits as enhanced? As we shall explain, we conclude that the answer is: Yes."
  — In re Marriage of Lehman, 18 Cal.4th 169, 174 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1242627/in-re-marriage-of-lehman/)
  "The fact that a nonemployee spouse who owns a community property interest in an employee spouse’s retirement benefits owns a community property interest in the latter’s retirement benefits as enhanced does not mean that the enhancement is a community asset in its entirety."
  — In re Marriage of Lehman, 18 Cal.4th 169, 180 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1242627/in-re-marriage-of-lehman/)
  Known gap: This clause states the holding of one 1998 California Supreme Court decision about one kind of employer-provided enhancement to a defined benefit plan; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension, and it does not state how any other post-separation change to a retirement benefit — a different incentive program, a disability election, a severance payment, or a benefit under a defined contribution plan — would be characterized. Lehman itself notes that decisions in this area have reached inconsistent results and that it disapproved a contrary suggestion in In re Marriage of Gram (1994) 25 Cal.App.4th 859 about adding putative service years to the time-rule denominator; that disapproval is not quoted here. The decision drew a dissent, which is not quoted. Both quotations were verified against two independent fetches of the CourtListener opinion page made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets; the same optical-character-recognition defects noted in this document's time-rule clause appear elsewhere in that text, and the passages quoted here were chosen from defect-free portions. No non-CourtListener copy of the opinion was obtained, and no pinpoint page is asserted for the first quotation because it appears in the opinion's introductory statement of the issue, before the first page break marked in the available text.

THE GILLMORE ELECTION — WHEN THE EMPLOYEE SPOUSE IS ELIGIBLE TO RETIRE BUT KEEPS WORKING
In In re Marriage of Gillmore (1981) 29 Cal.3d 418, the employee spouse became eligible to retire and draw a monthly pension but chose to continue working, and the trial court refused to order him to begin paying the other spouse her community share. The California Supreme Court held that this was an abuse of discretion. Reasoning that one spouse cannot defeat the other's community interest by invoking a condition wholly within his own control, the court stated that the employee spouse could not time his retirement so as to deprive the other spouse of an equal share of the community's interest in the pension, and that a unilateral choice to postpone retirement cannot be manipulated to impair the other spouse's interest in the benefits. The result is what practitioners call a "Gillmore election": once the employee spouse is eligible to retire, the nonemployee spouse may choose to receive that share immediately rather than wait. Summarizing Gillmore fifteen years later, the court in In re Marriage of Cornejo (1996) 13 Cal.4th 381 described the resulting sequence of choices — the employee spouse first chooses whether to retire or keep working, the nonemployee spouse then has a choice of delayed benefits or immediate payment, and the employee spouse has a final choice of satisfaction or avoidance.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Under the cases and statutory law, Earl cannot time his retirement to deprive Vera of an equal share of the community’s interest in his pension."
  — In re Marriage of Gillmore, 29 Cal.3d 418, 423 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1271657/in-re-marriage-of-gillmore/)
  "He will not forfeit his benefits if he leaves his employment voluntarily, is terminated or retires. The only condition precedent to payment of the benefits is his retirement, a condition totally within his control. A unilateral choice to postpone retirement cannot be manipulated so as to impair a spouse’s interest in those retirement benefits."
  — In re Marriage of Gillmore, 29 Cal.3d 418, 423 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1271657/in-re-marriage-of-gillmore/)
  "In brief, the employee spouse has an initial choice of retiring or continuing to work. He is not permitted, however, to adversely affect the nonemployee spouse’s share by putting off his retirement."
  — In re Marriage of Cornejo, 13 Cal.4th 381, 383 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1801910/in-re-marriage-of-cornejo/)
  "Thus, the nonemployee spouse has a choice of delayed benefits or immediate payment. If she decides on the latter, the employee spouse is given another choice. He may make arrangements to meet her demand for immediate payment; or he may simply retire and allow her to draw her share. In a word, the employee spouse has a final choice of satisfaction or avoidance."
  — In re Marriage of Cornejo, 13 Cal.4th 381, 383 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1801910/in-re-marriage-of-cornejo/)
  Known gap: This clause states the holding of a 1981 California Supreme Court decision and a later decision's summary of it; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension, and it does not state whether any person is eligible to retire, whether an election has been made, or what any share would be. Gillmore involved benefits that were both vested and matured under a private employer's plan, and the opinion's reasoning rests on the fact that the sole remaining condition on payment was the employee spouse's own retirement decision; the opinion does not address benefits that are not yet payable for reasons outside that spouse's control. Gillmore was decided under former Civil Code section 4800, the predecessor of the current Family Code division cited elsewhere in this document. Every quotation in this clause was verified against two independent fetches of the corresponding CourtListener opinion page made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets, and one Gillmore phrase and one Cornejo phrase were additionally confirmed by exact-phrase searches restricted to those opinions' clusters in CourtListener's public search API; no non-CourtListener copies of these opinions were obtained. Source-quality caution: the CourtListener text of Gillmore contains visible optical-character-recognition defects in other passages, including a footnote rendered as "if he retires or' loses his job" and a stray doubled period; the sentences quoted here were chosen from passages free of such defects. The names in the quoted sentences are the Gillmore parties' own.

WHO PAYS A GILLMORE ELECTION — THE EMPLOYEE SPOUSE, NOT THE PLAN
Gillmore does not force the employee spouse to retire. The court stated that he is free to continue working, but that if he does so he must reimburse the other spouse for the share of community property she loses as a result of that decision, and that if he does not wish to retire he must pay her an amount equivalent to her interest. The court also addressed the objection that this reaches the employee spouse's separate property, observing that the employee spouse alone makes the decision to use separate property for that purpose, when and if he decides not to retire, and comparing the situation to a spouse who keeps a community home and buys out the other's interest with separate funds. This allocation matters because California statutory law separately limits what a court may order the plan itself to do: Family Code section 2610 provides that a court shall not order a retirement plan to pay benefits to a party at any time before the member retires, except as provided in paragraph (3) of subdivision (a), unless the plan so provides.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "He is free to continue working. However, if he does so, he must reimburse Vera for the share of the community property that she loses as a result of that decision."
  — In re Marriage of Gillmore, 29 Cal.3d 418, 427 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1271657/in-re-marriage-of-gillmore/)
  "Earl alone will make the decision to use separate property to reimburse Vera, when and if he decides not to retire."
  — In re Marriage of Gillmore, 29 Cal.3d 418, 427 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1271657/in-re-marriage-of-gillmore/)
  "Here, Earl must divide his retirement benefits with Vera. If he does not wish to retire, he must pay her an amount equivalent to her interest."
  — In re Marriage of Gillmore, 29 Cal.3d 418, 427 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1271657/in-re-marriage-of-gillmore/)
  "Make the payment of benefits to a party at any time before the member retires, except as provided in paragraph (3) of subdivision (a), unless the plan so provides."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2610(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 2610(b)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2610)
  Known gap: This clause combines a 1981 California Supreme Court decision with a current California statute; they are independent sources, but the statute postdates the decision, which was issued under former Civil Code section 4800, so the statute is quoted here for the present-day limit it states rather than as the rule Gillmore applied. The same statutory subdivision is quoted in this corpus's separate information sheet on the division of retirement benefits and QDROs, so that document and this clause are not independent of each other as to the statutory point. This is one state's law and is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension or plan. The clause does not state what form a payment would take in any case — Gillmore mentions both a lump-sum buyout of the present value and monthly payments as possibilities — and it does not address how federal law governing private-sector plans, or the separate public-retirement-system mechanism referenced in paragraph (3) of subdivision (a) of section 2610, would apply. The Gillmore quotations were verified against two independent fetches of the CourtListener opinion page made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets; the statutory text was verified against two independent fetches of the California Legislative Information page for section 2610 made with two different browser User-Agent strings, which returned identical section text. The names in the quoted sentences are the Gillmore parties' own.

WHAT AN ELECTION OF IMMEDIATE PAYMENT GIVES UP
Gillmore describes the choice facing the nonemployee spouse as a genuine trade-off rather than a free option. The court noted that a nonemployee spouse may choose to wait, preferring to receive the retirement benefits when the employee spouse actually retires, thereby ensuring some protection for the future and possibly sharing in the increased value of the pension plan. If instead the nonemployee spouse chooses to receive immediate payments, the court stated that he or she has a right to do so. But in a footnote the court added that the nonemployee spouse cannot have it both ways: quoting In re Marriage of Luciano (1980) 104 Cal.App.3d 956, it described the decision to ask for distribution before the employee spouse actually retires as an irrevocable election to give up increased payments in the future that might accrue from increased age, longer service, and a higher salary, and stated that a spouse who takes her share immediately forfeits her right to share in the future increased value of those benefits.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "For example, the nonemployee spouse may choose to wait, preferring to receive the retirement benefits when the employee spouse actually retires. The nonemployee may thereby ensure some protection for the future and may be able to share in the increased value of the pension plan."
  — In re Marriage of Gillmore, 29 Cal.3d 418, 428 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1271657/in-re-marriage-of-gillmore/)
  "However, if the nonemployee spouse chooses to receive immediate payments, as Vera does, he or she has a right to do so. Any inequities caused by the immediate distribution of retirement benefits can be resolved through adjustments in spousal support."
  — In re Marriage of Gillmore, 29 Cal.3d 418, 428 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1271657/in-re-marriage-of-gillmore/)
  "The nonemployee spouse, of course, cannot have it both ways. The decision to ask for distribution of the retirement benefits before the employee spouse actually retires “constitutes an irrevocable election to give up increased payments in the future which might accrue due to increased age, longer service and a higher salary.”"
  — In re Marriage of Gillmore, 29 Cal.3d 418, 428, fn. 9 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1271657/in-re-marriage-of-gillmore/)
  Known gap: This clause states what one 1981 California Supreme Court opinion says about the consequences of electing immediate payment; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension, and it does not state whether waiting or electing would produce a larger or smaller total for any person — that depends on facts about the specific plan, the employee spouse's future service and compensation, and how long each spouse lives. The strongest statement of the trade-off appears in a footnote of the opinion, which quotes a Court of Appeal decision, so the "irrevocable election" language originates in In re Marriage of Luciano rather than in the Supreme Court's own text; the quotation below preserves the internal quotation marks of the original. The names in the quoted sentences are the Gillmore parties' own. Both quotations were verified against two independent fetches of the CourtListener opinion page made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets; no non-CourtListener copy of the opinion was obtained. This clause does not address whether or how parties may agree between themselves to a different arrangement, which Gillmore elsewhere notes is frequently done by settlement.

FROM WHAT DATE IMMEDIATE PAYMENTS RUN — IN RE MARRIAGE OF CORNEJO
Gillmore establishes the right to immediate payment but does not state the date from which those payments begin to accrue. In re Marriage of Cornejo (1996) 13 Cal.4th 381 answered that question. The California Supreme Court framed the issue as: if the employee spouse continues to work and the nonemployee spouse chooses immediate payment, as of what date is she entitled to obtain such payment. It considered four candidate dates — the date of eligibility to retire, the date of an informal demand preceding a motion, the date the motion is filed, and the date the court issues its order — and held that the correct answer is the date on which the nonemployee spouse files a motion seeking immediate payment, reasoning that the filing is a bright and formal act that puts the employee spouse on notice of his own choice of satisfaction or avoidance. The court stated that a nonemployee spouse is not entitled to premotion payment, and it rejected the argument that eligibility alone starts the clock as too early, noting that a spouse could otherwise face a claim accrued retroactively over a long period.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "The question presented is this: If the employee spouse continues to work, and the nonemployee spouse chooses immediate payment, as of what date is she entitled to obtain such payment?"
  — In re Marriage of Cornejo, 13 Cal.4th 381, 383 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1801910/in-re-marriage-of-cornejo/)
  "After review, we believe that the correct answer is the date on which the nonemployee spouse files a motion seeking immediate payment. Such a point in time is bright."
  — In re Marriage of Cornejo, 13 Cal.4th 381, 385 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1801910/in-re-marriage-of-cornejo/)
  "As explained, a nonemployee spouse is not entitled to premotion payment."
  — In re Marriage of Cornejo, 13 Cal.4th 381, 387 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1801910/in-re-marriage-of-cornejo/)
  Known gap: This clause states the holding of a 1996 California Supreme Court decision; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension, and it does not state whether any motion has been filed or what any payment would be. The decision drew a dissent, which would have run payments from the date of a written, unequivocal demand rather than from the filing of a motion; that dissent is not quoted here and was not the holding. Cornejo concerned a public retirement system, the State Teachers' Retirement System, and the majority distinguished two earlier decisions, In re Marriage of Gillmore and In re Marriage of Crook (1992) 2 Cal.App.4th 1606, as factually distinguishable and not controlling on the premotion question; this clause does not state how the rule would interact with a written agreement between spouses reached without any motion. All three quotations were verified against two independent fetches of the CourtListener opinion page made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets, and one of them was additionally confirmed by an exact-phrase search restricted to that opinion's cluster in CourtListener's public search API; no non-CourtListener copy of the opinion was obtained. The pronouns in the quoted sentences track the Cornejo parties' own circumstances.

SPOUSAL SUPPORT IS NOT A SUBSTITUTE FOR THE COMMUNITY SHARE
Both Brown and Gillmore address the argument that any unfairness from how a pension is handled can be cured through spousal support instead. Brown answered that alimony lies within the discretion of the trial court and that a spouse should not be dependent on that discretion to provide the equivalent of what should be hers as a matter of absolute right. Gillmore made the related point about financial circumstances: the courts are statutorily required to divide community property equally, the retirement benefit must first be divided equally, and a party may then renew a motion for modification of spousal support in light of that new distribution of community property. Read together, the two decisions treat the community share of a pension as a property right that is determined first, with support questions addressed afterward and separately.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Alimony, however, lies within the discretion of the trial court; the spouse "should not be dependent on the discretion of the court ... to provide her with the equivalent of what should be hers as a matter of absolute right.""
  — In re Marriage of Brown, 15 Cal.3d 838, 848 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1367330/in-re-marriage-of-brown/)
  "A court may consider the equities of the parties’ financial situations in determining spousal support, but only after the community property has been equitably divided. The retirement benefit must first be divided equally. Earl may then renew his motion for a modification of spousal support in light of this new distribution of the community property."
  — In re Marriage of Gillmore, 29 Cal.3d 418, 428 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1271657/in-re-marriage-of-gillmore/)
  Known gap: This clause states what two California Supreme Court opinions say about the relationship between property division and spousal support; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular case, and it does not state whether support would be ordered, modified, or terminated for anyone. Both opinions predate the current Family Code: Brown (1976) and Gillmore (1981) were decided under former Civil Code section 4800, and the equal-division requirement they describe now appears in a different statutory location. The Brown passage quoted here is itself a quotation of In re Marriage of Peterson (1974) 41 Cal.App.3d 642, so the language originates with the Court of Appeal; the quotation preserves the original internal quotation marks and the original ellipsis. Gillmore, in a passage quoted in this document's clause on the consequences of an election, separately states that inequities caused by immediate distribution can be resolved through adjustments in spousal support — a statement about adjusting support after the property division, not about substituting support for the community share. Both quotations were verified against two independent fetches of the corresponding CourtListener opinion pages, made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets; no non-CourtListener copies of these opinions were obtained.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A COURT FILING
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for background use alongside an actual dissolution of marriage or legal separation proceeding pending, concluded, or to be filed, in the California superior court for Sacramento County. It does not itself divide, value, or apportion any retirement benefit of Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee, does not make or preserve any election of immediate payment, and is not a motion; only the court — or the parties' own written agreement, where the law permits one — can address those matters.]

expectedJSON.body: This Pension Apportionment and Gillmore Election Information Sheet concerns Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, whose proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties is pending, has concluded by judgment, or may be filed, in the California superior court for Sacramento County. It describes what California law says about two related questions that arise when one spouse has earned retirement benefits under a defined benefit pension plan: first, how a court decides what portion of those benefits the community owns, including the apportionment method commonly called the "time rule"; and second, what happens when the employee spouse becomes eligible to retire but keeps working — the situation addressed in In re Marriage of Gillmore (1981) 29 Cal.3d 418, from which the phrase "Gillmore election" takes its name. It states, in general terms, the rule of In re Marriage of Brown (1976) 15 Cal.3d 838 that pension rights earned during marriage are community property whether or not they are vested, the division methods Brown describes and the continuing jurisdiction they require, the apportionment discussion in In re Marriage of Lehman (1998) 18 Cal.4th 169, the choices Gillmore gives each spouse once the employee spouse is eligible to retire, the statutory limit in Family Code section 2610 on ordering a plan to pay before the member retires, the consequences Gillmore attaches to an election of immediate payment, and the rule of In re Marriage of Cornejo (1996) 13 Cal.4th 381 fixing the date from which such payments run. This information sheet does not calculate any community or separate percentage, value any pension, state whether Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee is eligible to retire, or state whether any election has been made or any motion has been filed; those are matters for the court to decide on the specific evidence before it, or for Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee to address by their own written agreement.

California treats a pension right earned through employment during marriage as a property interest of the community rather than as a mere expectancy. In In re Marriage of Brown (1976) 15 Cal.3d 838, the California Supreme Court overruled French v. French (1941) 17 Cal.2d 775 and held that pension rights, whether or not vested, represent a property interest, and that to the extent those rights derive from employment during marriage they are a community asset subject to division in a dissolution proceeding. Brown also explains the specialized meaning the word "vested" carries in marital-property cases: it refers to a pension right that is not subject to forfeiture if the employment relationship ends before retirement. Under that usage a pension right may be vested — safe from forfeiture — and still not yet "matured," because the employee has not reached the point at which benefits are payable.

citations.quote: Pension rights, whether or not vested, represent a property interest; to the extent that such rights derive from employment during coverture, they comprise a community asset subject to division in a dissolution proceeding.
it refers to a pension right which is not subject to a condition of forfeiture if the employment relationship terminates before retirement.
Throughout our decisions we have always recognized that the community owns all pension rights attributable to employment during the marriage.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the holding and terminology of a 1976 California Supreme Court decision; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension, and pension characterization rules differ among community property and equitable distribution states. The Brown opinion was decided under former Civil Code section 4800, the predecessor of the Family Code provisions cited elsewhere in this document, so its statutory references do not match current section numbers. All three quotations were verified against two independent fetches of the CourtListener opinion page made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets, and the first quotation was additionally confirmed by an exact-phrase search restricted to that opinion's cluster in CourtListener's public search API; no non-CourtListener copy of this 1976 opinion was obtained, because the California courts' own website does not publish slip opinions from that era. Federal law separately governs whether and how a private-sector plan may pay a former spouse, and nothing in Brown displaces those federal requirements. This clause does not state what portion of any particular pension the community owns; that is the separate question of apportionment addressed in the clause that follows on the time rule.

expectedJSON.body: Brown describes two general approaches a court may take to a community interest in a pension. One is to determine the present value of the pension rights and divide that value now, often by awarding the pension to the employee spouse and offsetting other community assets to the other spouse. The other is used when uncertainties affecting vesting or maturation make present valuation unsatisfactory: the court awards each spouse an appropriate portion of each pension payment as it is paid, which avoids computing present value and divides equally the risk that the pension will never vest. Brown acknowledges that an award of future pension payments as they fall due requires the court to continue jurisdiction to supervise those payments. Brown's treatment of retroactivity also turns on reserved jurisdiction: the decision states that it does not apply retroactively to permit a nonemployee spouse to assert an interest in nonvested pension rights where the marriage's property rights were already adjudicated by a decree that became final, unless the decree expressly reserved jurisdiction to divide those pension rights later.

citations.quote: But if the court concludes that because of uncertainties affecting the vesting or maturation of the pension that it should not attempt to divide the present value of pension rights, it can instead award each spouse an appropriate portion of each pension payment as it is paid. This method of dividing the community interest in the pension renders it unnecessary for the court to compute the present value of the pension rights, and divides equally the risk that the pension will fail to vest.
As respondent points out, an award of future pension payments as they fall due will require the court to continue jurisdiction to supervise the payments of pension benefits.

We conclude that our decision today should not apply retroactively to permit a nonemployee spouse to assert an interest in nonvested pension rights when the property rights of the marriage have already been adjudicated by a decree of dissolution or separation which has become final as to such adjudication, unless the decree expressly reserved jurisdiction to divide such pension rights at a later date

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states what one 1976 California Supreme Court opinion says about division methods and continuing jurisdiction; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension, and it does not state which method a court would choose in any given case — Brown leaves that choice to the trial court. The retroactivity passage quoted here concerns the retroactive reach of the Brown decision itself to dissolution decrees that were final in 1976, not a general rule about reopening judgments today; relief from a final family law judgment is governed by separate provisions addressed elsewhere in this corpus. Brown predates the Retirement Equity Act of 1984 and the qualified domestic relations order mechanism, so its description of how payments reach a nonemployee spouse does not account for the federal requirements that now apply to private-sector plans. All three quotations were verified against two independent fetches of the CourtListener opinion page made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets; no non-CourtListener copy of the opinion was obtained. Part of the first quotation also appears, as a quotation of Brown, in In re Marriage of Gillmore, and a portion of it is quoted in this corpus's separate information sheet on the division of retirement benefits and QDROs, so it is not an independent source from that document's treatment of the same point.

expectedJSON.body: When a pension was earned partly during marriage and partly outside it, the benefit must be apportioned between the community estate and the employee spouse's separate estate. In In re Marriage of Lehman (1998) 18 Cal.4th 169, the California Supreme Court stated that the superior court must apportion an employee spouse's retirement benefits between the community property interest of the two spouses and any separate property interest of the employee spouse alone, that the court has discretion in the choice of methods, and that whatever method it uses the result must be reasonable and fairly representative of the relative contributions of the community and separate estates. The method Lehman describes as the one apparently employed most frequently is the time rule: the community property interest is expressed as a fraction whose numerator is the employee spouse's length of service during marriage before separation and whose denominator is the employee spouse's length of service in total, with the separate property interest being the remainder of 100 percent. Under a division of the community interest in halves, each spouse's share is one-half of the resulting community percentage.

citations.quote: The superior court must apportion an employee spouse’s retirement benefits between the community property interest of the employee spouse and the nonemployee spouse and any separate property interest of the employee spouse alone.

the community property interest in retirement benefits is the percentage representing the fraction whose numerator is the employee spouse’s length of service during marriage before separation, here 17.39 years, and whose denominator is the employee spouse’s length of service in total, here 32.67 years; the separate property interest is the percentage representing the remainder of 100 percent minus the community property interest percentage.

When, in a case such as this, the superior court uses the time rule, with the employee spouse’s length of service during marriage before separation in the numerator, and with the employee spouse’s length of service in total in the denominator, it arrives at a result that is “reasonable and fairly representative of the relative contributions of the community and separate estates.”

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states what one California Supreme Court opinion says about apportionment method; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension, and it does not compute or assert any percentage for any person. Lehman itself notes that the choice of apportionment method rests in the trial court's discretion, so the time rule is not the only permissible approach, and Lehman states that the time rule's use is not unreasonable where the amount of the retirement benefits is substantially related to the number of years of service — a condition that is a question of fact about the particular plan. This clause also fills a gap that this corpus's existing information sheet on the division of retirement benefits and QDROs expressly disclosed: that document states it does not describe the time-rule apportionment formula. Source-quality caution: the CourtListener text of this 1998 opinion contains visible optical-character-recognition defects, rendering the words "time rule" as "time rale" in several places and "born" as "bom"; the sentences quoted here were selected from passages free of such defects and were compared character for character across two independent fetches made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets, and one quoted phrase was additionally confirmed by an exact-phrase search restricted to that opinion's cluster in CourtListener's public search API. No non-CourtListener copy of the opinion was obtained. The percentages and year figures appearing in the quoted passage are the facts of the Lehman parties' own case and say nothing about any other marriage.

expectedJSON.body: Lehman also addressed what happens when an employer improves a defined benefit pension after the marriage has ended — in that case a voluntary early-retirement incentive that added putative years of service and waived an actuarial reduction. The court framed the question as whether a nonemployee spouse who owns a community property interest in an employee spouse's retirement benefits under such a plan owns a community property interest in the retirement benefits as enhanced, and answered yes. Lehman distinguishes two distinct questions: characterization, meaning whether the enhancement is a community asset at all, and apportionment, meaning to what extent it belongs to the community and separate estates. The court held that owning a community interest in the benefits carries with it a community interest in the benefits as enhanced, while cautioning that this does not mean the enhancement is a community asset in its entirety, because the extent of the community and separate shares remains a question of apportionment.

citations.quote: Does a nonemployee spouse who owns a community property interest in an employee spouse’s retirement benefits under such a plan own a community property interest in the retirement benefits as enhanced? As we shall explain, we conclude that the answer is: Yes.

The fact that a nonemployee spouse who owns a community property interest in an employee spouse’s retirement benefits owns a community property interest in the latter’s retirement benefits as enhanced does not mean that the enhancement is a community asset in its entirety.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the holding of one 1998 California Supreme Court decision about one kind of employer-provided enhancement to a defined benefit plan; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension, and it does not state how any other post-separation change to a retirement benefit — a different incentive program, a disability election, a severance payment, or a benefit under a defined contribution plan — would be characterized. Lehman itself notes that decisions in this area have reached inconsistent results and that it disapproved a contrary suggestion in In re Marriage of Gram (1994) 25 Cal.App.4th 859 about adding putative service years to the time-rule denominator; that disapproval is not quoted here. The decision drew a dissent, which is not quoted. Both quotations were verified against two independent fetches of the CourtListener opinion page made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets; the same optical-character-recognition defects noted in this document's time-rule clause appear elsewhere in that text, and the passages quoted here were chosen from defect-free portions. No non-CourtListener copy of the opinion was obtained, and no pinpoint page is asserted for the first quotation because it appears in the opinion's introductory statement of the issue, before the first page break marked in the available text.

expectedJSON.body: In In re Marriage of Gillmore (1981) 29 Cal.3d 418, the employee spouse became eligible to retire and draw a monthly pension but chose to continue working, and the trial court refused to order him to begin paying the other spouse her community share. The California Supreme Court held that this was an abuse of discretion. Reasoning that one spouse cannot defeat the other's community interest by invoking a condition wholly within his own control, the court stated that the employee spouse could not time his retirement so as to deprive the other spouse of an equal share of the community's interest in the pension, and that a unilateral choice to postpone retirement cannot be manipulated to impair the other spouse's interest in the benefits. The result is what practitioners call a "Gillmore election": once the employee spouse is eligible to retire, the nonemployee spouse may choose to receive that share immediately rather than wait. Summarizing Gillmore fifteen years later, the court in In re Marriage of Cornejo (1996) 13 Cal.4th 381 described the resulting sequence of choices — the employee spouse first chooses whether to retire or keep working, the nonemployee spouse then has a choice of delayed benefits or immediate payment, and the employee spouse has a final choice of satisfaction or avoidance.

citations.quote: Under the cases and statutory law, Earl cannot time his retirement to deprive Vera of an equal share of the community’s interest in his pension.

He will not forfeit his benefits if he leaves his employment voluntarily, is terminated or retires. The only condition precedent to payment of the benefits is his retirement, a condition totally within his control. A unilateral choice to postpone retirement cannot be manipulated so as to impair a spouse’s interest in those retirement benefits.
In brief, the employee spouse has an initial choice of retiring or continuing to work. He is not permitted, however, to adversely affect the nonemployee spouse’s share by putting off his retirement.

Thus, the nonemployee spouse has a choice of delayed benefits or immediate payment. If she decides on the latter, the employee spouse is given another choice. He may make arrangements to meet her demand for immediate payment; or he may simply retire and allow her to draw her share. In a word, the employee spouse has a final choice of satisfaction or avoidance.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the holding of a 1981 California Supreme Court decision and a later decision's summary of it; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension, and it does not state whether any person is eligible to retire, whether an election has been made, or what any share would be. Gillmore involved benefits that were both vested and matured under a private employer's plan, and the opinion's reasoning rests on the fact that the sole remaining condition on payment was the employee spouse's own retirement decision; the opinion does not address benefits that are not yet payable for reasons outside that spouse's control. Gillmore was decided under former Civil Code section 4800, the predecessor of the current Family Code division cited elsewhere in this document. Every quotation in this clause was verified against two independent fetches of the corresponding CourtListener opinion page made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets, and one Gillmore phrase and one Cornejo phrase were additionally confirmed by exact-phrase searches restricted to those opinions' clusters in CourtListener's public search API; no non-CourtListener copies of these opinions were obtained. Source-quality caution: the CourtListener text of Gillmore contains visible optical-character-recognition defects in other passages, including a footnote rendered as "if he retires or' loses his job" and a stray doubled period; the sentences quoted here were chosen from passages free of such defects. The names in the quoted sentences are the Gillmore parties' own.

expectedJSON.body: Gillmore does not force the employee spouse to retire. The court stated that he is free to continue working, but that if he does so he must reimburse the other spouse for the share of community property she loses as a result of that decision, and that if he does not wish to retire he must pay her an amount equivalent to her interest. The court also addressed the objection that this reaches the employee spouse's separate property, observing that the employee spouse alone makes the decision to use separate property for that purpose, when and if he decides not to retire, and comparing the situation to a spouse who keeps a community home and buys out the other's interest with separate funds. This allocation matters because California statutory law separately limits what a court may order the plan itself to do: Family Code section 2610 provides that a court shall not order a retirement plan to pay benefits to a party at any time before the member retires, except as provided in paragraph (3) of subdivision (a), unless the plan so provides.

citations.quote: He is free to continue working. However, if he does so, he must reimburse Vera for the share of the community property that she loses as a result of that decision.
Earl alone will make the decision to use separate property to reimburse Vera, when and if he decides not to retire.
Here, Earl must divide his retirement benefits with Vera. If he does not wish to retire, he must pay her an amount equivalent to her interest.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2610(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Make the payment of benefits to a party at any time before the member retires, except as provided in paragraph (3) of subdivision (a), unless the plan so provides.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause combines a 1981 California Supreme Court decision with a current California statute; they are independent sources, but the statute postdates the decision, which was issued under former Civil Code section 4800, so the statute is quoted here for the present-day limit it states rather than as the rule Gillmore applied. The same statutory subdivision is quoted in this corpus's separate information sheet on the division of retirement benefits and QDROs, so that document and this clause are not independent of each other as to the statutory point. This is one state's law and is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension or plan. The clause does not state what form a payment would take in any case — Gillmore mentions both a lump-sum buyout of the present value and monthly payments as possibilities — and it does not address how federal law governing private-sector plans, or the separate public-retirement-system mechanism referenced in paragraph (3) of subdivision (a) of section 2610, would apply. The Gillmore quotations were verified against two independent fetches of the CourtListener opinion page made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets; the statutory text was verified against two independent fetches of the California Legislative Information page for section 2610 made with two different browser User-Agent strings, which returned identical section text. The names in the quoted sentences are the Gillmore parties' own.

expectedJSON.body: Gillmore describes the choice facing the nonemployee spouse as a genuine trade-off rather than a free option. The court noted that a nonemployee spouse may choose to wait, preferring to receive the retirement benefits when the employee spouse actually retires, thereby ensuring some protection for the future and possibly sharing in the increased value of the pension plan. If instead the nonemployee spouse chooses to receive immediate payments, the court stated that he or she has a right to do so. But in a footnote the court added that the nonemployee spouse cannot have it both ways: quoting In re Marriage of Luciano (1980) 104 Cal.App.3d 956, it described the decision to ask for distribution before the employee spouse actually retires as an irrevocable election to give up increased payments in the future that might accrue from increased age, longer service, and a higher salary, and stated that a spouse who takes her share immediately forfeits her right to share in the future increased value of those benefits.

citations.quote: For example, the nonemployee spouse may choose to wait, preferring to receive the retirement benefits when the employee spouse actually retires. The nonemployee may thereby ensure some protection for the future and may be able to share in the increased value of the pension plan.

However, if the nonemployee spouse chooses to receive immediate payments, as Vera does, he or she has a right to do so. Any inequities caused by the immediate distribution of retirement benefits can be resolved through adjustments in spousal support.

The nonemployee spouse, of course, cannot have it both ways. The decision to ask for distribution of the retirement benefits before the employee spouse actually retires “constitutes an irrevocable election to give up increased payments in the future which might accrue due to increased age, longer service and a higher salary.”

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states what one 1981 California Supreme Court opinion says about the consequences of electing immediate payment; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension, and it does not state whether waiting or electing would produce a larger or smaller total for any person — that depends on facts about the specific plan, the employee spouse's future service and compensation, and how long each spouse lives. The strongest statement of the trade-off appears in a footnote of the opinion, which quotes a Court of Appeal decision, so the "irrevocable election" language originates in In re Marriage of Luciano rather than in the Supreme Court's own text; the quotation below preserves the internal quotation marks of the original. The names in the quoted sentences are the Gillmore parties' own. Both quotations were verified against two independent fetches of the CourtListener opinion page made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets; no non-CourtListener copy of the opinion was obtained. This clause does not address whether or how parties may agree between themselves to a different arrangement, which Gillmore elsewhere notes is frequently done by settlement.

expectedJSON.body: Gillmore establishes the right to immediate payment but does not state the date from which those payments begin to accrue. In re Marriage of Cornejo (1996) 13 Cal.4th 381 answered that question. The California Supreme Court framed the issue as: if the employee spouse continues to work and the nonemployee spouse chooses immediate payment, as of what date is she entitled to obtain such payment. It considered four candidate dates — the date of eligibility to retire, the date of an informal demand preceding a motion, the date the motion is filed, and the date the court issues its order — and held that the correct answer is the date on which the nonemployee spouse files a motion seeking immediate payment, reasoning that the filing is a bright and formal act that puts the employee spouse on notice of his own choice of satisfaction or avoidance. The court stated that a nonemployee spouse is not entitled to premotion payment, and it rejected the argument that eligibility alone starts the clock as too early, noting that a spouse could otherwise face a claim accrued retroactively over a long period.

citations.quote: The question presented is this: If the employee spouse continues to work, and the nonemployee spouse chooses immediate payment, as of what date is she entitled to obtain such payment?
After review, we believe that the correct answer is the date on which the nonemployee spouse files a motion seeking immediate payment. Such a point in time is bright.
As explained, a nonemployee spouse is not entitled to premotion payment.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the holding of a 1996 California Supreme Court decision; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular pension, and it does not state whether any motion has been filed or what any payment would be. The decision drew a dissent, which would have run payments from the date of a written, unequivocal demand rather than from the filing of a motion; that dissent is not quoted here and was not the holding. Cornejo concerned a public retirement system, the State Teachers' Retirement System, and the majority distinguished two earlier decisions, In re Marriage of Gillmore and In re Marriage of Crook (1992) 2 Cal.App.4th 1606, as factually distinguishable and not controlling on the premotion question; this clause does not state how the rule would interact with a written agreement between spouses reached without any motion. All three quotations were verified against two independent fetches of the CourtListener opinion page made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets, and one of them was additionally confirmed by an exact-phrase search restricted to that opinion's cluster in CourtListener's public search API; no non-CourtListener copy of the opinion was obtained. The pronouns in the quoted sentences track the Cornejo parties' own circumstances.

expectedJSON.body: Both Brown and Gillmore address the argument that any unfairness from how a pension is handled can be cured through spousal support instead. Brown answered that alimony lies within the discretion of the trial court and that a spouse should not be dependent on that discretion to provide the equivalent of what should be hers as a matter of absolute right. Gillmore made the related point about financial circumstances: the courts are statutorily required to divide community property equally, the retirement benefit must first be divided equally, and a party may then renew a motion for modification of spousal support in light of that new distribution of community property. Read together, the two decisions treat the community share of a pension as a property right that is determined first, with support questions addressed afterward and separately.

citations.quote: Alimony, however, lies within the discretion of the trial court; the spouse "should not be dependent on the discretion of the court ... to provide her with the equivalent of what should be hers as a matter of absolute right."

A court may consider the equities of the parties’ financial situations in determining spousal support, but only after the community property has been equitably divided. The retirement benefit must first be divided equally. Earl may then renew his motion for a modification of spousal support in light of this new distribution of the community property.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states what two California Supreme Court opinions say about the relationship between property division and spousal support; it is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular case, and it does not state whether support would be ordered, modified, or terminated for anyone. Both opinions predate the current Family Code: Brown (1976) and Gillmore (1981) were decided under former Civil Code section 4800, and the equal-division requirement they describe now appears in a different statutory location. The Brown passage quoted here is itself a quotation of In re Marriage of Peterson (1974) 41 Cal.App.3d 642, so the language originates with the Court of Appeal; the quotation preserves the original internal quotation marks and the original ellipsis. Gillmore, in a passage quoted in this document's clause on the consequences of an election, separately states that inequities caused by immediate distribution can be resolved through adjustments in spousal support — a statement about adjusting support after the property division, not about substituting support for the community share. Both quotations were verified against two independent fetches of the corresponding CourtListener opinion pages, made with two different browser User-Agent and Accept-Language header sets; no non-CourtListener copies of these opinions were obtained.
